title: TensorFlow and Keras
summary: TensorFlow with Keras is the other major deep learning framework, widely used in production and on mobile/edge via TensorFlow Lite. Keras offers a clean, high-level API that lets you build and train models with very little code. Knowing both PyTorch
content:
# TensorFlow and Keras ##### The model that needed to run on a phone A team built an excellent plant-disease classifier in PyTorch. Farmers would photograph a leaf and get a diagnosis. Accuracy was strong. Then came deployment. The users were in rural areas with intermittent connectivity, so the model had to run **on the device**, offline, on budget Android phones with limited memory. Converting a PyTorch model to a mobile runtime in 2020 meant exporting to ONNX, converting to TensorFlow, then to TensorFlow Lite, debugging unsupported operations at each hop. It took three weeks. A colleague pointed out that building it in Keras would have made deployment a four-line conversion, because TensorFlow Lite is part of the same ecosystem. That is the honest case for knowing both frameworks. PyTorch dominates research and general-purpose work; **TensorFlow's advantage has always been the deployment ecosystem** — TF Lite for mobile and embedded, TF.js for browsers, TF Serving for production APIs. Knowing which to reach for is a real engineering decision. ##### Keras: the Sequential API Keras is TensorFlow's high-level API, and it is genuinely the fastest way to express a standard model. ```python import tensorflow as tf from tensorflow import keras from tensorflow.keras import layers model = keras.Sequential([ layers.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1)), layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255), # preprocessing IN the model layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu", padding="same"), layers.BatchNormalization(), layers.MaxPooling2D(), layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same"), layers.BatchNormalization(), layers.MaxPooling2D(), layers.Flatten(), layers.Dropout(0.4), layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10), # logits, no softmax ], name="mnist_cnn") model.summary() ``` Compare this with the PyTorch equivalent from yesterday. There is no `forward` method, no manual flattening, no explicit shape arithmetic — Keras infers shapes from the input specification and reports them in `summary()`. For a straightforward feedforward stack, that is a real productivity gain. Note `layers.Rescaling` inside the model. Putting preprocessing into the graph means it travels with the exported model, so the deployment target does not need to replicate your normalization — which is exactly the kind of detail that makes mobile deployment painless. ##### The Functional API `Sequential` handles linear stacks. For anything with branches, multiple inputs, or skip connections, the **Functional API** treats layers as callables on tensors: ```python def residual_block(x, filters): """A skip connection — impossible to express with Sequential.""" shortcut = x y = layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, padding="same")(x) y = layers.BatchNormalization()(y) y = layers.ReLU()(y) y = layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, padding="same")(y) y = layers.BatchNormalization()(y) y = layers.Add()([y, shortcut]) # the residual connection return layers.ReLU()(y) # Multi-input model: images plus tabular metadata image_input = keras.Input(shape=(64, 64, 3), name="image") meta_input = keras.Input(shape=(8,), name="metadata") x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")(image_input) x = layers.MaxPooling2D()(x) x = residual_block(x, 32) x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x) m = layers.Dense(16, activation="relu")(meta_input) combined = layers.Concatenate()([x, m]) combined = layers.Dropout(0.3)(combined) output = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="prediction")(combined) model = keras.Model(inputs=[image_input, meta_input], outputs=output) ``` The pattern is `output_tensor = LayerClass(config)(input_tensor)` — you instantiate a layer, then call it on a tensor. This makes arbitrary graphs expressible while keeping Keras's shape inference and `summary()`. A third option, **model subclassing**, mirrors PyTorch's style almost exactly: subclass `keras.Model`, define layers in `__init__`, implement `call()`. Use it when you need genuinely dynamic control flow. ##### Compile and fit This is where Keras differs most from PyTorch. Instead of writing a training loop, you **configure** one: ```python model.compile( optimizer=keras.optimizers.AdamW(learning_rate=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4), loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy", keras.metrics.SparseTopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3)], ) history = model.fit( train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=50, callbacks=callbacks, verbose=1, ) ``` Three choices in `compile` deserve attention. **`from_logits=True`** tells the loss that your final layer outputs raw scores rather than probabilities. This is the same numerical-stability point as PyTorch's `BCEWithLogitsLoss` — the loss applies softmax internally using a stable formulation. Applying softmax in the model *and* setting `from_logits=True` is a common bug that quietly degrades accuracy. **`SparseCategoricalCrossentropy`** takes integer labels (`3`); the non-sparse version expects one-hot vectors. Choosing the wrong one produces a shape error at best and wrong training at worst. **Metrics are computed for you** across the epoch, which is a genuine convenience compared with accumulating counters manually. The `fit` call handles batching, shuffling, the training loop, validation, progress display and callbacks. For standard supervised learning that is perhaps 60 lines of PyTorch replaced by one call — the clearest illustration of the two frameworks' philosophies. ##### Callbacks Callbacks hook into the training loop at defined points, and they are Keras's mechanism for everything a custom loop would otherwise do explicitly: ```python callbacks = [ keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping( monitor="val_loss", patience=8, restore_best_weights=True, # roll back to the best epoch verbose=1, ), keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint( "checkpoints/best.keras", monitor="val_accuracy", save_best_only=True, verbose=1, ), keras.callbacks.ReduceLROnPlateau( monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=4, min_lr=1e-6, verbose=1, ), keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir="logs/run1", histogram_freq=1), keras.callbacks.CSVLogger("training_log.csv"), ] ``` `restore_best_weights=True` is important and easy to miss: without it, early stopping leaves you with the *last* epoch's weights rather than the best, which is usually a few epochs past the optimum. Custom callbacks are straightforward when you need something specific: ```python class LogGradientNorm(keras.callbacks.Callback): def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None): lr = float(self.model.optimizer.learning_rate) print(f" epoch {epoch}: lr={lr:.2e} val_loss={logs['val_loss']:.4f}") ``` ##### tf.data `tf.data` is TensorFlow's input pipeline, and it is one of the ecosystem's genuine strengths — it builds an optimized, parallelized data graph: ```python AUTOTUNE = tf.data.AUTOTUNE train_ds = ( tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_train, y_train)) .shuffle(buffer_size=10_000, reshuffle_each_iteration=True) .batch(64) .map(augment_fn, num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE) # parallel augmentation .prefetch(AUTOTUNE) # overlap CPU prep with GPU compute .cache() ) val_ds = ( tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((X_val, y_val)) .batch(128) .prefetch(AUTOTUNE) ) ``` **`prefetch(AUTOTUNE)`** is the single highest-value line: it prepares the next batch on the CPU while the GPU processes the current one, which frequently eliminates data-loading as a bottleneck. `AUTOTUNE` lets TensorFlow choose the buffer sizes and parallelism dynamically. Order matters. Shuffle before batching (otherwise you shuffle batches, not samples), and cache after any expensive deterministic preprocessing but before random augmentation. ##### Saving and serving This is where the ecosystem argument lives. ```python # Modern Keras format — architecture + weights + optimizer state model.save("model.keras") loaded = keras.models.load_model("model.keras") # Weights only model.save_weights("weights.weights.h5") # SavedModel — the format TF Serving, TF Lite and TF.js consume model.export("saved_model/") ``` **TensorFlow Lite** for mobile and embedded — the problem from the opening story: ```python converter = tf.lite.TFLiteConverter.from_saved_model("saved_model/") converter.optimizations = [tf.lite.Optimize.DEFAULT] # dynamic-range quantization # Full int8 quantization needs a representative dataset for calibration def representative_data(): for images, _ in val_ds.take(100): yield [tf.cast(images, tf.float32)] converter.representative_dataset = representative_data converter.target_spec.supported_ops = [tf.lite.OpsSet.TFLITE_BUILTINS_INT8] converter.inference_input_type = tf.uint8 converter.inference_output_type = tf.uint8 tflite_model = converter.convert() open("model.tflite", "wb").write(tflite_model) ``` Quantization converts `float32` weights to `int8`, typically shrinking the model roughly fourfold and speeding up inference on mobile CPUs, with modest accuracy loss. That block of code is the entire mobile deployment path — four weeks of work in the opening story reduced to a conversion step. **TensorFlow Serving** handles production APIs with versioning, batching and gRPC: ```bash docker run -p 8501:8501 \ --mount type=bind,source=$(pwd)/saved_model,target=/models/classifier \ -e MODEL_NAME=classifier -t tensorflow/serving ``` **TensorFlow.js** runs models directly in a browser, and **TFX** provides production ML pipelines with data validation and model analysis. ##### PyTorch versus TensorFlow/Keras | | PyTorch | TensorFlow / Keras | |---|---|---| | **Style** | Imperative, explicit loops | Declarative, `compile` + `fit` | | **Debugging** | Standard Python — print, pdb | Harder inside graph mode | | **Flexibility** | Excellent for custom research | Excellent for standard architectures | | **Boilerplate** | More (you write the loop) | Less | | **Research adoption** | Dominant | Minority | | **Mobile / embedded** | ExecuTorch, improving | **TF Lite — mature** | | **Browser** | Limited | **TF.js — mature** | | **Serving** | TorchServe | **TF Serving — mature** | | **Pretrained models** | HuggingFace ecosystem | Keras Applications, TF Hub | The framework war has largely settled. **PyTorch won research and general development**; TensorFlow retained deployment breadth, and Keras 3 now runs on PyTorch, TensorFlow or JAX backends, which blurs the line further. When to pick each, concretely: **Choose PyTorch when** you are doing research or custom architectures, using HuggingFace models, need step-through debugging, or joining a team that already uses it — which most do. **Choose TensorFlow/Keras when** you must deploy to mobile or embedded devices via TF Lite, need to run in a browser, want the fastest path for a standard architecture, or are working in an organization already invested in TFX and TF Serving. The reassuring reality: **the concepts transfer completely.** Tensors, autodiff, layers, losses, optimizers, batching, callbacks — every idea from the PyTorch day has a Keras equivalent. Learning the second framework takes days, not weeks. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Model needed] --> B{Deployment target?} B -->|mobile / embedded| C[Keras → TF Lite
+ quantization] B -->|browser| D[Keras → TF.js] B -->|server API| E{Team preference} B -->|research / custom| F[PyTorch] E -->|TF shop| G[Keras → TF Serving] E -->|otherwise| F C & D & G & F --> H[Same concepts:
tensors, autodiff, layers,
losses, optimizers] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **Softmax in the last layer *and* `from_logits=True`** — double application, degraded training. - **`CategoricalCrossentropy` with integer labels** instead of the `Sparse` version. - **`EarlyStopping` without `restore_best_weights=True`**, keeping the wrong epoch. - **Shuffling after batching**, which shuffles batch order rather than samples. - **No `prefetch`**, leaving the GPU waiting on data. - **Shuffling the validation dataset** — pointless and confusing for debugging. - **Saving only weights** when you need the full model, then failing to reconstruct the architecture. - **Skipping the representative dataset** for int8 quantization, causing large accuracy loss. - **Assuming a PyTorch model converts cleanly** to mobile formats — plan the deployment target early. - **Learning only one framework** and being unable to read the other's code, which rules out a great deal of published work. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **build the same image classifier from the PyTorch day using Keras**, with **callbacks for early stopping and checkpointing**. Building the identical model twice is the point — you will see that `compile` plus `fit` replaces your entire training loop, and that the concepts map one to one. Note where each framework felt easier; that judgment is what the comparison is for. The mini project is a **Keras model for a tabular or image dataset with callbacks, saved and reloaded for inference**. Then go one step further than the brief and **convert it to TFLite with quantization**, comparing file size and accuracy before and after. Seeing a 12 MB model become 3 MB with a 0.4% accuracy drop is the concrete argument for the TensorFlow deployment story. For the assignment, **compare PyTorch and TensorFlow/Keras on API style and describe a scenario for each**. Ground it in specifics rather than preference: PyTorch's explicit loop gives you a breakpoint anywhere and is why research code is written in it; Keras's `fit` plus callbacks removes boilerplate for standard training and connects directly to TF Lite, TF.js and TF Serving. Then give a real scenario each — an offline mobile diagnostic app versus a novel architecture with custom gradient flow — and say which you would choose and why. ##### Key takeaways - Keras `Sequential` handles linear stacks with automatic shape inference; the Functional API expresses branches, skip connections and multi-input models. - `compile` plus `fit` replaces a hand-written training loop, with callbacks providing early stopping, checkpointing, LR scheduling and logging. - Use `from_logits=True` with a logits output layer, and match `Sparse` versus one-hot loss variants to your label format. - `tf.data` with `prefetch(AUTOTUNE)` keeps the GPU fed; shuffle before batching and cache before random augmentation. - TensorFlow's real advantage is the deployment ecosystem — TF Lite, TF.js and TF Serving — so choose the framework partly by where the model must run.
